data.title: Martyrdom, Religious Difference, and “Fear” as a Category of Piety in the Sasanian Empire: The Case of the Martyrdom of Gregory and the Martyrdom of Yazdpaneh
data.abstractNote: This study examines the disproportionately heavy reliance on the word dehḷtā (“fear”) and its cognates in two related sixth-century Syriac martyr texts from the Sasanian Empire, and how this usage refl ects both an acknowledgement of and an attempt to transcend the religious diversity of the sixth century. It begins by describing the contents and historical background of the two martyrdoms and highlighting their broad, even elastic, usage of dehḷtā and its cognates. The origins of the wide semantic range of dehḷtā are attributed to Syriac translation literature, especially the Peshitta, the Syriac version of the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament. After a survey of how this term appears in earlier East Syrian martyr acts, the study turns to the close engagement with Zoroastrianism found in the martyrdoms of Gregory and Yazdpaneh and then to an examination of how “fear” relates to the texts’ theological and ethical concerns. It is suggested that fear is an embodied form of knowledge evoked in these texts at the same time that it operates in the textual process of coercion that creates religious subjects.

data.title: Mor Gabriel aus Beth Qusṭan: Leben und Legende eines syrischen Abtbischofs aus dem 7. Jahrhundert
data.abstractNote:
Abbot-Bishop Mor Gabriel, born in 593 in Beth Qustan, is the most famous son of the Tur Abdin, the “Mountain of the Servants (of God),” a region in south-eastern Anatolia. The most common form of name given to the monastery, built in 397 and one of the most respected and wealthiest foundations in the orient, refers to him. Mor Gabriel is famous for his miracles and, now as then, binds people together across confessional and religions boundaries.
This book offers the first annotated German translation of the Syrian Life of Mor Gabriel. The author, himself a native of Beth Qustan, has based his work on a thorough study of the sources. He takes into account oral as well as literary traditions and subjects contradictory reports to historical criticism. Many illustrations of the monastery and the original manuscripts complete the work

data.abstractNote: «En 769, un Syrien nommé Cyrus souffrit le martyre en Osroène en raison de sa foi chrétienne. Deux textes syriaques traitent de cet événement: un récit, long mais aujourd'hui fragmentaire, originellement écrit par le Chroniqueur de Zuqin en 774, et une très courte notice dans la Chronique de Michel le Syrien (XIIe siècle). Le présent article s'efforce de reconstituer le récit fragmentaire, en retraçant la vie du martyr à l'aide de sources syriaques et arabes, et réfute l'assertion de Michel le Syrien selon laquelle Cyrus embrassa l'Islam avant de revenir ensuite, au prix de sa vie, à la foi chrétienne.» (Résumé du périodique, p. 317)

data.title: Révélations de Macaire et de Marc de Tarmaqa sur le sort de l’âme après la mort
data.abstractNote: "Les deux textes syriaques édités ci-après [ms. Vaticano (Città del), Biblioteca apostolica Vaticana, "Vat." sir. 96, f. 113v-121], une Vision de Macaire ["Visio de sorte animarum"] et une Vision de Marc de Tarmaqa ["Visio de sorte animarum"], tout en se rattachant à l'Egypte, présentent le sort de l'âme dans l'attente du jugement sous un tout autre jour. Durant ce laps de temps, aucune puisssance infernale ne la menace ni ne la moleste, elle n'est plus en butte à l'assaut des démons, sa route n'est plus semée de périls variés. Par contre, on voit apparaître une étroite connexion entre les pérégrinations de l'âme dans l'Au-delà et la liturgie funéraire." "Dialogue entre Macaire et le crâne d'un prêtre égyptien païen, crâne qu'il avait trouvé sur sa route. Voici cette historiette telle que la rapporte la recension sahidique conservée par le ms. copte I. B. 17, no 484 de la Bibliothèque nationale de Naples." (pp. 161-162; 188)

data.title: Saint ‘Azzīza et son village de Zérīni
data.abstractNote: "L'histoire de Mar 'Azziza n'apporte pour ainsi dire rien à l'hagiographie, sauf que l'un des disciples de l'Aonés de Sozomène se retrouve au Hakkari nestorien avec une légende qui lui attribue Mar Awgin comme maître. Comme tout moine qui se respecte était forcément disciple de Mar Awgin, ceci ne fournit pas d'argument nouveau pour l'identification ou la distinction d'Awgin et d'Aonés. Plus intéressant est l'apport du colophon. On y trouve un des rares témoignages sur la vie et les fouffrances d'un village de la montagne nestorienne aux XVe et XVIe siècles." (p. 433)

data.title: Some Further Notes on Thecla in Syriac Christianity
data.abstractNote: This paper is a follow up to an earlier publication in which data related to the Syriac Acts of Thecla and to the cult of Thecla in Syria were provisionally collected and surveyed. Some further data are presented here. They are taken from Syriac literary sources: the letters of Severus of Antioch, a liturgical hymn, and the biography of John of Tella. In addition, the Armenian tradition of the Acts of Thecla is briefly mentioned as a witness to the early Syriac text.

data.title: St. George: The Indigenous Foreigner in Kerala Christianity
data.abstractNote: The cult of St. George in Kerala, South India, brought initially by Syrian merchants, bolstered by Portuguese and British colonizers, and currently called into question by the Vatican, represents a complex entanglement of cultural and colonial forces. Informed by post-colonial theories which argue for the hybridization of colonized cultures, this paper presents Kerala's St. George cult as reflecting an ambivalent stance toward foreign influences and impositions. In spite of hybrid St. George's occasional expedient association with imperial powers, however, I argue that this European-looking saint is, in the eyes of most of his devotees, uninterested in foreign affairs and, ultimately, a champion for indigenous concerns.

data.title: Studies in the Syriac Versions of St. John Chrysostom’s Homilies on the New Testament, with Special Reference to Homilies 6, 20, 22, 23, 37, 62, 83 and 84 on John
data.abstractNote: Systematic study of the Syriac version of C’s homilies on the New Testament – Matthew, John and epistles of Paul; focuses mainly on 6th and 7th century British Library mss, which preserve translation from the 5th and 6th centuries; analysis of translation methods allows placement of version within framework of development of Syriac translation technique and highlighting of methodological issues that arise when relating Syriac versions to their Greek source texts; anlaysis shows that the homilies on the epistles translated last and most literal; those on Matthew and John translated earlier, relatively less literal and most likely to have Peshitta or even on occason Old Syriac bible texts rather than translation from the Greek. Several homilies on John edited and translated allowing a critique of Boismard’s interpretation and use of the Syriac version, which seen to be unsatisfactory in several ways.
